To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the performance of an algorithm depends on the type of the input document collection and the characteristics of the system.

1) for small document collections, the inverted index algorithm performs best; 2) for large document collections, the algorithm that uses the document collection performs best; 3) the algorithm that uses a document collection is more robust to changes in the system characteristics and query input; and 4) the algorithm that processes joins by using the document collection is more efficient in processing queries that have a large number of terms in the join condition

the performance of the three algorithms depends on the type of the input document collection, the system characteristics, and the input query; and that the algorithm that is likely to be the most effective depends on the type and characteristics of the input document collections and the input query.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (a) What is the relative performance of the algorithms for processing joins? (b) What are the characteristics of input document collections and queries for which the algorithms perform best? (c) What are the implications for the design of database systems that support joins on attributes of textual type?
the following questions: (1) What is the best algorithm to use to process joins between textual attributes?
the problem of processing joins on textual attributes in large databases and the results of this research are useful in designing systems for information retrieval and database applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the algorithm which performs well on the input document collection and on the input query is the one to be used.
the choice of the algorithm depends on the input data set and the system configuration.
the algorithm that uses the inverted files performs best for large document collections and the algorithm that uses documents performs best for medium-sized document collections.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best algorithm is the one that uses the inverted file to process the join, but this algorithm performs poorly when the input document collection contains documents of small size.

the inverted file based algorithm is likely to outperform the document based algorithm, and that the document based algorithm is likely outperform the inverted file based one, depending on the input document collection and the query.
the algorithm which uses document collections to process the join should be the algorithm of choice if the input document collection is small or medium sized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no one best algorithm for all types of input data and all query types.
the choice of the algorithm to use to process the join should be made dynamically, depending on the input document collection and query characteristics.
, in the absence of knowledge about the input document collection, it is not possible to identify the best algorithm for processing joins between attributes of a textual data type.
